headline: A headmaster’s challenge to his male students: Speak up about rape
author: Casey Parks

paragraphs.text: Usually, Stephen Beatty opens the Monday morning assemblies with a dad joke or two. He’s the headmaster of Royal St. George’s College, an all-boys school in Toronto, and he likes to start the school week with a bit of fun.

But as news broke that a former Cornell University student had accused seven fraternity members of sexually assaulting her while she was incapacitated, Beatty told his faculty he needed to hold a different kind of assembly this week.

Maybe the boys could tell, as Beatty held the door open, that this assembly would be different. They kept their phones in their pockets. They found seats in the 136-year-old Anglican chapel without so much as a snicker.

Beatty had known most of them since they were young enough to cry over lost pets and dying grandparents. He’d celebrated when they earned their yellow belts in judo. He’d read to them every Friday in his office when they were 8. But they were teenagers now, and it was his job to help usher them into adulthood.
“Gentlemen,” he said, “I want to talk with you today about something difficult.”

Beatty knew how badly his students wanted to blend in. They all wore the same blue blazers with the school’s crest embroidered on the front. They kept their ties loose at the neck. Most had the same fuzzy haircut that reminded Beatty of an alpaca. They were good boys, he thought. He couldn’t imagine any of them committing the kinds of sexual acts that might get them arrested. But he wanted — he needed — to ask more from them.

As he stood at the pulpit, Beatty thought of a comment he’d seen online. People had been calling the accused fraternity brothers “the Cornell 7.” One woman noted on Instagram that allegedly 50 other young men had been in a Snapchat group where a man invited them to participate in the assault. She called them “the Cornell 57.”
“Not one had the courage to stop this,” Beatty said. “They stayed silent.”

Beatty scanned the crowd. The boys had their eyes locked on him. They didn’t fidget. They were listening. Beatty told his boys he wanted to talk about that silence. “School is about learning. And perhaps the most important thing you are learning is about yourself,” he said, then asked: “What kind of man do you want to be?”
BEATTY HAD GIVEN a version of this speech twice before.

He’d first talked to his students about rape more than a decade ago after two football players in Steubenville, Ohio, were convicted of sexually assaulting a high school girl, while others videoed the acts and posted clips to social media. Beatty gave a second version of the speech in 2024 after a woman said she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of Hockey Canada’s junior championship team. The players were found not guilty last year, but Beatty remained troubled by the circumstances — multiple men were involved, and the woman was intoxicated.

When Beatty read about the Cornell case, he felt the same outrage. He wasn’t sure if he had anything new to say, though. Then a few of his female colleagues told him they hoped he would speak up again.
He couldn’t live with himself, he decided, if he didn’t take every opportunity to teach the 350 boys in his charge how to be.

Beatty is 59 — “An old man,” he calls himself — but he remembered how hard it was to be a teenage guy. He’d attended Royal St. George’s in the 1970s and ‘80s, and he’d yearned then for guidance. Once, after his best friend died in an amusement park accident, Beatty had walked, grief-stricken, to a teacher’s home to ask how to survive the loss.

That teacher had helped Beatty navigate the hardest times of his life. Beatty wanted to be that kind of mentor, but as he considered what to say about Cornell, he worried his students would feel labeled as bad just because they’re boys. Beatty didn’t want them to feel painted into the corner of toxic masculinity. Shame would not inspire them.

All weekend, Beatty fretted over what to say. He talked to his 92-year-old father and his college-aged sons, then, Sunday night, he carried his laptop down to his basement, turned on the Buffalo Bills football game, muted it, and began to write.
I am horrified.

He took his hands off the keyboard. Earlier that semester, he’d watched one of his boys, a giant baseball player, embroider flowers in art class. He’d watched other boys recite poetry. He’d traveled to the woods with them, and he’d listened as they talked about their parents, their fears, the secret struggles they rarely revealed.
I know your kindness, your sense of fairness, and the care you show for one another. I believe in you.

Beatty knew good people could falter in terrible situations. As a teenager, he’d watched without protest as his peers bullied an overweight boy. He knew decent people could remain silent even when they knew something wasn’t right. He knew how safe silence could feel.
I know. Boys, please believe me, I know.

BEATTY WROTE LATE into the night. He read the speech again and again, and he canceled his early morning appointments. He was nervous, but as he stood at the pulpit Monday morning and looked out at his boys, that anxiety disappeared. They were listening.

Beatty thought often of the overweight boy he grew up with. He’d known as a young man that his silence hurt that boy, but Beatty had thought he was protecting himself. In the decades since, he’d realized that silence had corroded him, too. Silence numbed young men, he knew now. It stopped them from asking for help. It left them feeling alone.
“Silence can be framed as some manly quality. The strong silent type. Don’t believe that,” he told the boys. “It is not strong.”
“What is truly masculine and strong is breaking silence,” he continued. “We need to be brave. Not silent. Decide that the man you are and the man you will be will not be silent.”

In his years as headmaster, Beatty had learned that you can’t just tell a boy what not to do. You have to give him clear instructions. And so he told the students to think of his speech as a fire drill — practice for a real emergency. If someone makes a degrading joke about a girl, the boys should say, “That’s enough.” If a boy shares a private photograph of a girl, the recipient should reply, “Don’t send me that. Delete it.”

“What would you do when a group chat turns cruel, or a friend starts talking about someone as though she is a prize to be won or a possession to be had?” he asked his audience. “Do you join in? Do you stay quiet because you don’t want to make things awkward?”

Beatty encouraged the boys to make things awkward. If they witnessed an assault, they needed to do everything in their power to stop it. They needed to be loud. They could break a window, pull a fire alarm. They could call their parents, or they could call him.

He told them to pull out their cellphones, then he gave them his number. Use it, he told them. Use it when you don’t know what to do. Use it when you need someone to help without judgment or consequence. He told them that he loved them.
”I know you,” he told them. “I know that’s the kind of man you want to be and the kind of man you will be.”

Beatty sometimes joked that there’s nothing profound in boys. They could be deep and substantive, but they weren’t usually complex in their expression. A few grunted “Nice speech, sir” as they filed out of the chapel. Others thanked him in the cafeteria that afternoon.

When he got back to his office, he saw most had already texted him. They were short messages. More than one had written only, “Hey, Mr. Beatty, it’s me.” Still, Beatty felt emotional. His boys were saying something. For now, that was enough.
